title: Part 6, Chapter 2
paragraphs: "Ah, these cigarettes!" Porfiry Petrovitch exclaimed at last, having lit one. "They're terrible for you, absolutely terrible, and yet I can't quit! I cough, my throat tickles, I can't breathe properly. You know, I'm a coward — I went to see Dr. B— recently. He gives every patient at least half an hour. He actually laughed when he examined me. He tapped my chest and said: 'Tobacco is bad for you — your lungs are affected.' But how am I supposed to quit? What would I replace it with? I don't drink — that's the problem, he-he-he — that I don't drink. Everything is relative, Rodion Romanovitch — everything is relative!"

"Here he goes with his professional tricks again," Raskolnikov thought with disgust. All the details of their last meeting suddenly came flooding back, along with the same feeling that had overwhelmed him then.

"I actually came to see you the day before yesterday, in the evening — you didn't know?" Porfiry Petrovitch continued, looking around the room. "I came right into this very room. I was passing by, just like today, and I thought I'd return your visit. I walked in — your door was wide open — looked around, waited, and left without giving my name to your servant. Don't you lock your door?"
Raskolnikov's expression grew darker and darker. Porfiry seemed to read his mood.
"I've come to have it out with you, Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow! I owe you an explanation and I must give it to you," he continued with a slight smile, patting Raskolnikov's knee lightly.

But almost at the same instant a serious, careworn look came over his face. To his surprise, Raskolnikov saw a hint of sadness in it. He had never seen or suspected such an expression on Porfiry's face.

"A strange scene took place between us last time, Rodion Romanovitch. Our first meeting was strange too, but then... well, one thing after another! Here's the point: I may have treated you unfairly, and I feel it. Do you remember how we parted? Your nerves were shot, your knees were shaking — and so were mine. And you know, the way we behaved wasn't very civil, wasn't gentlemanly at all. And yet we are gentlemen — above all else, gentlemen. That has to be acknowledged. You remember where things ended up between us?... It was quite improper."
"What is he up to? What does he take me for?" Raskolnikov asked himself in amazement, raising his head and looking straight at Porfiry.

"I've decided that honesty is the best policy between us," Porfiry Petrovitch continued, turning his head away and lowering his eyes, as though unwilling to unsettle his former quarry, as though disdaining his old tricks. "Yes, such suspicions and such scenes can't go on forever. It was Nikolay who put a stop to it — otherwise I don't know where we might have ended up. That damned workman was sitting in the next room the whole time — you can picture that? You know that, of course; and I'm aware he came to see you afterward. But what you believed at the time was wrong: I hadn't sent for anyone, I hadn't made any arrangements. You ask why? Well, what can I say — it all happened so suddenly. I'd barely had time to send for the building porters — you noticed them on your way out, I'm sure. An idea flashed through my mind: I was firmly convinced at the time, you see, Rodion Romanovitch. I thought — even if I let one thing slip for the moment, I'll catch something else. At least I won't lose what matters. You're nervously irritable by temperament, Rodion Romanovitch — out of all proportion to your other qualities of heart and character, which I flatter myself I've partly figured out. Of course, even then I realized that a person doesn't always just stand up and blurt out their whole story. It happens sometimes, if you push someone past the breaking point — but it's rare. I understood that much. What I needed was just one fact, even the smallest concrete detail — something I could hold on to, something tangible, not just psychology. Because if a person is guilty, you should be able to get something solid out of them — you can sometimes get the most astonishing results. I was counting on your temperament, Rodion Romanovitch — on your temperament above all. I had great hopes for you."
"But what are you driving at now?" Raskolnikov finally muttered, asking the question almost without thinking.
"What is he talking about?" he wondered, bewildered. "Does he really believe I'm innocent?"

"What am I driving at? I've come to explain myself — I consider it my duty, so to speak. I want you to understand clearly how the whole business, the whole misunderstanding, developed. I've caused you a great deal of suffering, Rodion Romanovitch. I'm not a monster. I understand what it means for someone who's been through hardship but who is proud, imperious, and above all impatient to endure such treatment! In any case, I regard you as a man of noble character, with elements of genuine magnanimity — though I don't agree with all your views. I wanted to tell you this first, frankly and sincerely, because above all I don't want to deceive you. When I first met you, I felt drawn to you. Perhaps you'll laugh at that. You have every right to. I know you disliked me from the start, and you have no reason to like me. Think what you will — but I want now to do everything I can to erase that impression and show you that I'm a man with a heart and a conscience. I mean it."
Porfiry Petrovitch paused with dignity. Raskolnikov felt a wave of renewed alarm. The idea that Porfiry believed him innocent was starting to make him uneasy.

"There's hardly any need to go through everything in detail," Porfiry Petrovitch went on. "I couldn't, really. To start with, there were rumors. Through whom, how, and when they reached me... and how they implicated you — I don't need to get into all that. My suspicions were triggered by a complete accident, one that might easily never have happened. What was it? Hmm! I think there's no need to go into that either. All those rumors and that accident led me to one idea. I'll admit it openly — I was the first one to fix on you. The old woman's notes about the pledges and so forth — that all came to nothing. Yours was one among a hundred. I also happened to hear about the scene at the police office — someone described it brilliantly, unconsciously recreating the scene with great vividness. It was just one thing after another, Rodion Romanovitch, one thing after another! How could I help arriving at certain conclusions? From a hundred rabbits you can't make a horse; a hundred suspicions don't make a proof — as the English proverb says. But that's pure rationality, and you can't help being partial — a prosecutor is only human, after all. I also thought about your article in that journal — remember our first visit when we discussed it? I mocked you then, but that was only to draw you out. I repeat: you're ill, Rodion Romanovitch, and impatient. That you were bold, headstrong, serious, and had felt deeply — I recognized early on. I've felt the same things myself, so your article seemed familiar to me. It was conceived on sleepless nights, with a pounding heart, in ecstasy and suppressed passion. And that proud, suppressed passion in young people — it's dangerous! I mocked you then, but let me tell you: as a literary admirer, I'm very fond of such first efforts, full of youthful fire. There's a haze and a chord vibrating in the mist. Your article is absurd and fantastical, but there's a transparent sincerity in it, a youthful incorruptible pride, and the audacity of despair. It's a dark piece, but that's what makes it powerful. I read it, set it aside, and thought: 'That man won't take the ordinary path.' After such a preamble, how could I not be swept along by what followed? Oh, I'm not saying anything definitive — I'm making no statement now. I simply noted it at the time. 'What's really here?' I asked myself. Nothing! Possibly absolutely nothing. And it's really not proper for a prosecutor to let himself get carried away by notions: here I've got Nikolay on my hands, with real evidence against him — think what you like of it, but it is evidence. He brings his own psychology too; one has to take him into account — it's a matter of life and death. Why am I telling you all this? So you'll understand, and not blame me for my malicious behavior on that occasion. It wasn't malicious, I assure you, he-he! Do you think I didn't search your room at the time? Oh, I did — he-he! I was here while you lay ill in bed — not officially, not in person, but I was here. Your room was searched to the last thread at the first opportunity, but umsonst! I thought: now that man will come — will come to me on his own, and quickly too. If he's guilty, he's bound to come. Someone else wouldn't, but he will. And do you remember how Mr. Razumikhin started discussing the case with you? We arranged that to provoke you — so we deliberately spread rumors, knowing he'd bring them to you. Razumikhin can't restrain his indignation. Mr. Zametov was tremendously struck by your anger and your brazen daring. Think of it — blurting out in a restaurant: 'I killed her!' Too bold, too reckless. I thought at the time: if he's guilty, he'll be a formidable opponent. That's what I was thinking. I was expecting you. And you came! Oh, my heart was pounding. Ah!

"Now — why did you have to come? Your laughter as you entered — do you remember? I saw everything plainly. But if I hadn't been expecting you so keenly, I wouldn't have noticed anything in your laughter. You see the power of mood! And Mr. Razumikhin — ah, that stone, that stone under which the things were hidden! I can picture it somewhere in a kitchen garden. You told Zametov about a kitchen garden, and you repeated it in my office, didn't you? And when we started picking apart your article — how you explained it! Every word could be taken two ways, as though there were a hidden second meaning.

"And so, Rodion Romanovitch, I reached the limit — and smacked my head against a wall. I stopped myself and asked: what am I doing? After all, everything can be explained the other way too, if you want — and in fact more naturally. I had to admit it was more natural. I was tormented! 'No,' I thought, 'I need some concrete detail.' And when I heard about the doorbell-ringing, I held my breath and started trembling. 'Here's my concrete detail!' I thought — and I stopped thinking it over. I would have paid a thousand rubles at that moment to have seen you with my own eyes when you walked a hundred paces beside that workman after he called you a murderer to your face, and you didn't dare ask him a single question the whole way. And then the chills you described? The bell-ringing during your illness, in a half-delirious state?

"So, Rodion Romanovitch — is it any wonder I played those games with you? And what made you show up at that exact moment? It was as if someone had sent you, I swear! And if Nikolay hadn't interrupted us... Remember Nikolay at that moment? Remember him clearly? It was a thunderbolt, a real thunderbolt! And how did I react? I didn't believe the thunderbolt — not for one second. You could see that yourself. And later, when you'd left and Nikolay gave some very plausible answers on certain points — so plausible even I was surprised — even then I didn't believe his story! That's what it means to be firm as a rock! 'No,' I thought, 'not a chance. What has Nikolay got to do with it!'"
"Razumikhin just told me you believe Nikolay's guilty, that you told him so yourself..."

His voice failed him and he broke off. He had been listening in indescribable agitation as this man, who had seen through him completely, now seemed to be retracting everything. He was afraid to believe it and didn't believe it. In those still-ambiguous words he searched desperately for something more definite, more conclusive.

"Mr. Razumikhin!" Porfiry cried, as if delighted by a question from the previously silent Raskolnikov. "He-he-he! I had to get Mr. Razumikhin out of the way — two's company, three's a crowd. Razumikhin is the wrong person for this; besides, he's an outsider. He came running to me, white as a sheet... But never mind him — why bring him into it? Back to Nikolay: would you like to know what kind of man he is, as I understand him? First of all, he's still basically a child — and not exactly a coward, but something like an artist. Really, don't laugh at me for describing him that way. He's innocent, impressionable, and emotional. He has a heart, and he's a dreamer. He sings, dances, tells stories so well that people come from other villages to hear him. He goes to school and laughs until he cries if you hold up a finger at him. He'll drink himself unconscious — not as a vice, but when people treat him. He's like a child in that. And he steals too — without realizing it, because 'how can picking something up be stealing?' And did you know he's an Old Believer? Actually, more of a dissenter. There have been Wanderers in his family, and he spent two years in his village under the spiritual guidance of an elder. I learned all this from Nikolay himself and from people in his village. And what's more — he wanted to flee into the wilderness! He was full of religious fervor, prayed at night, read the old books — the 'true' ones — and read himself nearly out of his mind.
[A religious sect. — Translator's note.]

"Petersburg had a huge effect on him, especially the women and the wine. He's responsive to everything, and he forgot the elder and all that. I learned that an artist here took a liking to him and used to visit him. And then this whole business fell on him.

"Well, he was frightened — he tried to hang himself! He ran away! What can you do about the Russian people's terror of the legal system? The very word 'trial' scares some of them witless. Whose fault is that? We'll see what the new jury system does. God willing, it will help! Well, in prison he apparently remembered the venerable elder; the Bible reappeared too. Do you know, Rodion Romanovitch, what the word 'suffering' means to some of these people? It's not suffering for someone's benefit — it's simply: 'one must suffer.' To accept suffering — and if it comes from the authorities, so much the better. In my time, there was a very meek prisoner who spent an entire year reading his Bible on the stove at night, and he read himself crazy. So crazy that one day, for no reason at all, he grabbed a brick and flung it at the warden — even though the man had never done him any harm. And the way he threw it: deliberately aimed a yard to the side, for fear of actually hurting him. Well, you know what happens to a prisoner who assaults an officer with a weapon. So 'he accepted his suffering.'

"So now I suspect Nikolay wants to 'accept his suffering' — or something like it. I know it for a fact. Only he doesn't know that I know. What — you don't believe such people exist among the peasants? There are plenty. The elder has begun influencing him again, especially after the attempted hanging. But he'll come and tell me everything himself. You think he'll hold out? Just wait — he'll take back his confession. I'm expecting him any hour now to come and recant. I've grown fond of Nikolay and I'm studying him carefully. And you know what? He-he! On some points he answered me very plausibly — clearly he'd gathered some evidence and prepared himself. But on other points he's completely at sea, doesn't know a thing, and doesn't even suspect that he doesn't know!

"No, Rodion Romanovitch, Nikolay has nothing to do with this! This is a fantastical, dark, modern case — an incident of our times, when the human heart is troubled, when people quote the phrase that blood 'renews,' when comfort is preached as the aim of life. Here we have bookish dreams, a mind unhinged by theories. Here is determination in the first stage, but determination of a special kind: he decided to do it like jumping off a cliff or a bell tower, and his legs trembled as he walked to the crime. He forgot to shut the door behind him, yet murdered two people — all for a theory. He committed the murder but couldn't take the money; what he managed to grab, he hid under a stone. Suffering behind the door while they battered at it and rang the bell wasn't enough for him — no, he had to go back to the empty apartment, half-delirious, to relive the bell-ringing, to feel those cold shivers again... All right, we can chalk that up to illness. But consider this: he's a murderer, yet he sees himself as an honest man, despises others, poses as injured innocence. No — that's not the work of a Nikolay, my dear Rodion Romanovitch!"
Everything said before had sounded so much like a retraction that these words hit like a thunderbolt. Raskolnikov shuddered as though he'd been stabbed.
"Then... who then... is the murderer?" he asked in a strangled voice, unable to stop himself.
Porfiry Petrovitch sank back in his chair as though genuinely astonished by the question.
"Who is the murderer?" he repeated, as if unable to believe his ears. "Why, you are, Rodion Romanovitch! You are the murderer," he added, almost in a whisper, in a voice of absolute conviction.
Raskolnikov sprang from the sofa, stood for a few seconds, and sat back down without a word. His face twitched convulsively.

"Your lip is twitching again, just like before," Porfiry observed, almost sympathetically. "You've been misunderstanding me, I think, Rodion Romanovitch," he added after a brief pause. "That's why you're so shocked. I came specifically to tell you everything and deal with you openly."
"It wasn't me — I didn't murder her," Raskolnikov whispered, like a small child caught misbehaving.
"Yes, it was you, Rodion Romanovitch — you and no one else," Porfiry whispered sternly, with conviction.

They were both silent, and the silence lasted a strangely long time — about ten minutes. Raskolnikov put his elbow on the table and ran his fingers through his hair. Porfiry Petrovitch sat quietly, waiting. Finally Raskolnikov looked scornfully at Porfiry.
"You're back to your old tricks, Porfiry Petrovitch! The same old method. Don't you ever get tired of it?"

"Oh, forget all that — what does it matter now? Things would be different if there were witnesses present, but we're whispering alone. You can see for yourself that I haven't come to chase and trap you like a rabbit. Whether you confess or not makes no difference to me at this point. I'm convinced with or without it."
"If that's so, why did you come?" Raskolnikov asked irritably. "I'll ask you the same question again: if you consider me guilty, why don't you arrest me?"
"Well, that's quite a question! I'll answer point by point. First, arresting you outright isn't in my interest."
"How so? If you're convinced, you ought to..."

"Oh, so what if I'm convinced? For now, that's just my theory. Why should I lock you up where you'd be safe? You know that's exactly what it would mean — since you're asking for it yourself. If I put you in a lineup with that workman, for example, and you say to him, 'Were you drunk or not? Who saw me with you? I simply assumed you were drunk, and you were too' — well, what could I say to that? Especially since your version is more plausible than his, because his testimony is backed by nothing but psychology — which is almost indecent, given his ugly mug — while you'd hit the nail on the head, because the man is a notorious, confirmed drunkard. And I've admitted frankly several times already that this psychology business cuts both ways, and the second interpretation is the stronger one, much more convincing. And apart from that, I have nothing against you so far. True, I will arrest you, and I've actually come — quite against protocol — to warn you in advance. But I'm telling you honestly, also against protocol, that it won't be to my advantage. Well, secondly, I've come because..."
"Yes, yes — secondly?" Raskolnikov was listening breathlessly.

"Because, as I just told you, I consider I owe you an explanation. I don't want you to think of me as a monster, since I genuinely like you — believe it or not. And thirdly, I've come with a direct, open proposal: surrender and confess. It will be infinitely better for you — and easier for me too, since my task will be done. Now — is that open enough?"
Raskolnikov thought for a moment.
"Listen, Porfiry Petrovitch. You just said yourself you have nothing but psychology. Yet now you've jumped to mathematics. What if you're the one who's mistaken?"
"No, Rodion Romanovitch, I'm not mistaken. I have a small fact — even then Providence sent it to me."
"What small fact?"

"I won't tell you, Rodion Romanovitch. In any case, I don't have the right to put this off any longer — I must arrest you. So think it over: at this point it makes no difference to me, so I'm speaking purely for your benefit. Believe me — it will be better, Rodion Romanovitch."
Raskolnikov smiled bitterly.
"That's not just ridiculous — it's positively shameless. Even if I were guilty — which I don't admit — what possible reason would I have to confess, when you yourself tell me I'd be safer in prison?"

"Ah, Rodion Romanovitch, don't put too much faith in words. Perhaps prison won't be so restful after all. That's just a theory — my theory — and who am I as an authority? Perhaps I'm hiding something from you even now, he-he! And how can you ask what advantage there'd be? Surely you know how it would reduce your sentence! You'd be confessing at a moment when another man has taken the crime on himself and muddied the entire case. Think about that! I swear before God I'll arrange it so that your confession comes as a complete surprise. We'll sweep away all these psychological points, all the suspicion against you, so that your crime will look like an aberration — because in truth it was an aberration. I'm an honest man, Rodion Romanovitch, and I'll keep my word."
Raskolnikov sat in gloomy silence, his head bowed dejectedly. He thought for a long time and finally smiled again, but this time his smile was sad and gentle.
"No," he said, apparently dropping all pretense with Porfiry. "It's not worth it. I don't care about reducing the sentence."
"That's exactly what I was afraid of!" Porfiry cried with warmth that seemed almost involuntary. "That's precisely what I feared — that you wouldn't care about the reduction."
Raskolnikov looked at him sadly and expressively.
"Don't disdain life!" Porfiry went on. "You have so much of it ahead of you. How can you say you don't want a lighter sentence? You're an impatient man!"
"So much of what ahead of me?"
"Life! What kind of prophet are you? How much do you really know? Seek and you shall find. Perhaps this is God's way of bringing you to Him. And the imprisonment — it isn't forever..."
"The sentence will be reduced," Raskolnikov laughed.
"Is it middle-class disgrace you're afraid of? Maybe you're afraid of it without realizing it, because you're young! But in any case, you of all people shouldn't be afraid to surrender and confess."
"Oh, damn it all!" Raskolnikov whispered with loathing and contempt, as though unwilling to speak aloud.
He stood up again as if meaning to leave, but sank back down in obvious despair.

"Damn it, if you like! You've lost faith and you think I'm just crudely flattering you. But how long have you been alive? How much do you understand? You invented a theory and then were ashamed when it fell apart and turned out not to be at all original! True, it turned out to be something base — but you're not hopelessly base. Not at all! At least you didn't deceive yourself for long: you went straight to the furthest extreme in one leap. How do I see you? I see you as one of those men who could stand there smiling while someone cuts out their entrails — if only they'd found faith or God. Find it, and you'll live. You've needed a change of direction for a long time now. Suffering is a good thing, too. Suffer! Maybe Nikolay is right in wanting to suffer. I know you don't believe it — but don't overthink it. Just throw yourself straight into life, without calculating. Don't be afraid — the current will carry you to shore and set you on your feet. What shore? How would I know? I only believe you have a long life ahead of you. I know you take all my words now for a prepared speech, but perhaps you'll remember them later. They might be useful sometime. That's why I'm saying them. It's lucky you only killed the old woman. If you'd come up with a different theory, you might have done something a thousand times more monstrous. You ought to thank God, perhaps. How do you know — maybe God is saving you for something. Keep your spirits up and be less afraid! Are you frightened by the great atonement ahead? No, it would be shameful to shrink from it. Since you've taken such a step, you must steel yourself. That's justice. Do what justice demands. I know you don't believe it, but truly — life will see you through. In time you'll accept it. What you need right now is fresh air — fresh air — fresh air!"
Raskolnikov actually flinched.
"Who are you? What kind of prophet are you? From what height of serene authority do you pronounce these words of wisdom?"

"Who am I? I'm a man with nothing left to hope for, that's all. A man with perhaps some feeling and sympathy, maybe even some knowledge — but whose day is past. You, though — you're a different matter. There's a life waiting for you. Though who knows — maybe your life will drift away in smoke too. What does it matter that you'll enter a different class of men? It's not comfort you'll miss, not with your heart! What does it matter if no one sees you for a long time? It's not about time — it's about yourself. Be the sun, and everyone will see you. The sun must be the sun, first and foremost. Why are you smiling again — because I'm such a Schiller? I bet you think I'm trying to win you over with flattery. Well, maybe I am, he-he-he! Maybe you'd better not take my word for it — maybe you should never fully believe me. I'm built that way, I confess. But you can judge for yourself how far I'm base and how far I'm honest."
"When do you plan to arrest me?"
"I can give you another day or two to walk around. Think it over, my dear fellow, and pray to God. It's in your interest, believe me."
"And what if I run?" Raskolnikov asked with a strange smile.

"You won't run. A peasant would run; a fashionable follower of someone else's ideology would run — show him the tip of your finger and he'll believe anything for the rest of his life. But you've already stopped believing in your theory. What would you run away with? And what would you do in hiding? It would be hateful, difficult — and what you need more than anything is a definite position, a proper atmosphere. And what atmosphere would you find? If you ran, you'd come back on your own. You can't manage without us. And if I put you in prison — say for a month, two, three — mark my words: you'll confess of your own accord, and you may even surprise yourself. You won't know an hour beforehand that you're about to confess. I'm convinced you'll decide to 'accept your suffering.' You don't believe me now, but you'll come to it. Because suffering, Rodion Romanovitch, is a great thing. Never mind that I've gotten fat — I understand that all the same. Don't laugh at it; there's an idea in suffering. Nikolay is right. No, you won't run, Rodion Romanovitch."
Raskolnikov stood up and took his cap. Porfiry Petrovitch rose as well.
"Going for a walk? The evening should be lovely — if we don't get a storm. Though a storm would clear the air nicely."
He too picked up his cap.

"Porfiry Petrovitch — please don't get the idea that I confessed to you today," Raskolnikov said with sullen insistence. "You're a strange man, and I listened to you out of simple curiosity. But I admitted nothing — remember that!"

"Oh, I know, I'll remember. Look at him — he's trembling! Don't worry, my dear fellow. Have it your way. Take a walk — just don't go too far. One last request, if I may," he added, lowering his voice. "It's an awkward one, but important. If by any chance — though I really don't believe it, and I think you're quite incapable of it — but just in case, during these forty or fifty hours, you were to get the notion of ending things some other way... in some violent fashion — laying hands on yourself..." (It's an absurd idea, but you must forgive me for it.) "Do leave a brief, clear note — just two lines — and mention the stone. It would be more generous. Well then — till we meet! Good thoughts and sound decisions to you!"

Porfiry left, stooping slightly and avoiding Raskolnikov's eyes. Raskolnikov went to the window and waited with irritated impatience until he judged Porfiry had reached the street and moved away. Then he too hurried out of the room.
